snippet.title: The 14th-Century Dental Tool Designed to Break Your Jaw
snippet.description:
Going to the dentist makes many of us anxious today, but taking a trip back to the Middle Ages reveals a true historical horror story. Long before the luxury of modern anesthetics, sterile clinics, and clean instruments, dealing with a simple toothache meant subjecting yourself to absolute agony.

This journey into the past exposes the brutal reality of medieval oral care, where practitioners treated cavities with lethal arsenic fillings and hunted imaginary "tooth worms" by stabbing raw dental nerves with red-hot cauterizing irons. You will witness the terrifying array of tools patients had to endure, including a jaw-snapping lever system that remained in use for centuries.

snippet.title: Advice for time traveling to medieval Europe
snippet.description:
Watch this video before visiting the European Middle Ages.

SUGGESTED READING

• Steven A. Epstein, An Economic and Social History of Later Medieval Europe, 1000–1500 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2009).
• Urban Tignor Holmes, Jr., Daily Living in the Twelfth Century (Madison: University of Wisconsin Press, 1952).
• Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (London: The Bodley Head, 2008).
• Paul B. Newman, Daily Life in the Middle Ages (Jefferson, N.C.: McFarland & Company, 2001).
• Jeffrey L. Singman, Daily Life in Medieval Europe (Westport, Conn.: Greenwood Press, 1999).


FAQ

• What about traveling there as a woman?
My advice applies to both men and women (except for the bit about clergy, obviously). Men and women will have to give the same amount of attention to constructing their backstory, including their marital status, because people will ask either way. Women went on pilgrimages. While most women (and men) worked on farms, women in towns did engage in economic activities like shopkeeping and weaving. It was rare for a woman to work as a long-distance merchant, but it did happen, typically as a widow whose husband had been a merchant.

• But what about a woman traveling alone?
When I said, "Travel in a group, don't travel alone," I meant it. Solo travel is not advised, regardless of gender. Even the medieval people themselves traveled in groups.


CORRECTIONS

• I said William of Rubruck was from the Netherlands but he was actually Flemish. Apologies to my Flemish viewers.
• In the anecdote where William of Rubruck met the Buddhist monks, he was confused at first but he did figure out in the course of talking to them that they were not Christian. I misremembered the passage. So I'd say Buddhists would probably just be understood as pagans in medieval Europe.
• The magic I discuss in the video is known as natural magic. There was also another form of magic I didn't talk about where you perform occult rituals to persuade demons to do things for you. That's known as demonic magic.

Though we often imagine the Middle Ages through the lens of romance and chivalry, the reality was far more brutal. Life expectancy rarely rose above 30 to 40 years, and most didn’t live past childhood. Those who did, walked a tightrope of dangers that neither prayer nor folk charm could fend off. It was a time when deadly threats lay waiting around every corner. Let’s travel back in time and take a look at just some of the grim ways in which the Medievals met their end.

snippet.title: 500 AD: The Ghost City Where 90% of the Population Vanished (Rome)
snippet.description:
Forget the burning ruins, apocalyptic wastelands, and endless barbarian hordes you see in Hollywood movies. If you stepped foot into actual Rome in the year 500 AD, the eerie silence of a hollowed-out metropolis would knock you flat. Discover the haunting, resilient, and fascinating reality of what people really ate, how they lived, and what they endured to survive in the twilight of the greatest city on Earth.

In this video, we cover:

The Ghost Metropolis: How a city built for over a million people transformed into a staggering, half-empty monument where nature slowly reclaimed the outer streets.

A Divided Capital: Why the native Roman elite and the new Ostrogothic rulers lived side-by-side but remained strictly segregated by culture, clothing.

The Post-Empire Diet: The reality of the surviving grain dole, the pungent garum fish sauce, and how Northern European meat-heavy tastes collided with classic Mediterranean staples.

Chariots and Chaos: The intense, high-speed fanaticism of the Circus Maximus, where tens of thousands still gathered to scream for their favorite racing factions.

If you enjoyed this deep dive into the 6th century, hit that Like button, Subscribe for more unvarnished history, and let me know in the comments: what historical era or city should we uncover next?

How Viking longhouses were designed to trap and circulate heat

The role of turf walls and earth insulation

What they stored to survive months without fresh food

How livestock, smoke, and shared living spaces created warmth

The winter routines that kept entire villages alive

It wasn’t chaos. It wasn’t constant raiding. It was structure, strategy, and survival systems refined over generations.

The real Viking winter story is far smarter and far more practical than the version most of us learned in school.

snippet.title: Versailles Palace in the 1600s: Why the Elites Used Staircases as Latrines
snippet.description:
When we think of King Louis XIV and his magnificent French court, we picture sparkling chandeliers, pristine silk gowns, and absolute luxury. But beneath the gold leaf and the glamorous facade of the 17th century lay a horrifyingly unhygienic reality. From aristocratic courtiers using grand staircases as latrines to elaborate powdered wigs crawling with lice, the absolute pinnacle of European wealth was actually a beautiful, gilded cesspool.

In this video, we strip away the Hollywood glamour to uncover the dark, dirty, and downright shocking daily life inside the most famous palace on Earth. Discover why the wealthiest people in the world absolutely refused to take a bath, how they tried to mask the suffocating stench of ten thousand unwashed bodies, and why surviving the royal doctors was sometimes harder than surviving the plague!

What this video covers:

The Plumbing Nightmare: Why the spectacular Palace of Versailles had zero flushing toilets, leading to corners and corridors becoming public latrines.

The Fear of Bathing: The bizarre 17th-century medical paranoia that made water the enemy, and how courtiers used "dry washing" instead.

Perfume over Puddles: How overwhelming animal-musk fragrances were used to combat the daily stench of human waste and sweat.

In a world without the internet, television, playlists on demand or even (for most people at least), books, the Medievals had to get creative about passing the time, because entertainment was pretty limited. Many turned to gambling games to alleviate the boredom. And, since Luck and Fortune never bothered to distinguish between the poor and the wealthy, medieval gambling had a reputation for being the downfall of just about everyone. 

Players didn’t just lose a few coins, they lost clothes, horses, entire estates, and in some spectacularly ill-advised cases, halves of kingdoms. 

Medieval dice (and later card games) weren’t just pastimes; they were high risk lifestyle choices that could turn a noble into a pauper faster than you could say ‘roll again.’

The simple soups and stews that formed the backbone of peasant diets

Cheap grains and breads that provided most daily calories

How people stretched small amounts of food to feed entire families

Preservation methods that made food last through winter

Why these dishes were simple… but surprisingly effective

No luxury ingredients. No modern kitchens. Just practical food that kept people going during hard times.

snippet.title: The First Black Death: How 50% of England Was Wiped Out in 541 AD
snippet.description:
When we think of the bubonic plague, our minds jump straight to the 1300s. But eight centuries earlier, an invisible phantom washed ashore, wiping out nearly half of Europe's population. How did the people of early England survive the very first global apocalypse?

Long before the towering stone castles and plague doctors of the late medieval era, the post-Roman world was devastated by the Plague of Justinian (541 AD). In this historical deep dive, we strip away the myths to uncover the gritty, exhausting reality of 6th-century Britain. From their complete lack of modern hygiene to the brutal necessity of sharing single-room, dirt-floor homes with livestock, we explore how the daily lives of these early farmers created the perfect breeding ground for a catastrophe.

What This Video Covers:

The harsh reality of daily life, farming, and survival in post-Roman Britain.

Sixth-century hygiene, primitive soap, and why families lived alongside their animals.

The terrifying arrival and rapid spread of the Plague of Justinian (Yersinia pestis).

How the immune survivors capitalized on the aftermath to fundamentally reshape the future of Medieval England.

Primary Sources & Further Reading:

To ensure accuracy, the historical facts and archaeological data in this video were compiled from the following peer-reviewed studies and historical texts:

Ancient Yersinia pestis genomes from across Western Europe (PNAS Study on Cambridgeshire DNA): pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1820447116

Dating the Justinianic Plague in England (Medieval Archaeology, 2024): tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00665983.2024.2419157

Procopius: History of the Wars (6th-Century Eyewitness Account): sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/source/542procopius-plague.asp

Bald's Leechbook (Early English Medicine & Herbal Poultices): cambridge.org/core/journals/anglo-saxon-england

West Stow Anglo-Saxon Village (Daily Life & Architecture): weststow.org/Anglo-Saxon-Village/

⚠ This documentary is created for educational and historical awareness. The content does not support or encourage hate, discrimination, or violence in any form. The purpose is to examine past events responsibly so that their mistakes are understood and never repeated.

The harsh reality of daily life, farming, and survival in post-Roman Britain.

Sixth-century hygiene, primitive soap, and why families lived alongside their animals.

snippet.title: D-Day: The Brutal 24 Hours That Changed the World
snippet.description:
The global landscape hung in the balance on a turbulent Tuesday morning in June 1944. Thousands of young men packed into pitching landing craft along the English Channel, completely unaware of the sheer scale of the nightmare awaiting them on the beaches of Normandy. Hitler's Atlantic Wall stood as a terrifying barrier of concrete, steel, and relentless machine-gun nests, meticulously designed to cut down any invading force within seconds of the landing ramps dropping.

This detailed account layout focuses on the raw personal stories of the ordinary people who found themselves thrust into the center of the conflict. From the scattered paratroopers navigating treacherous drops in pitch darkness to the infantry units facing absolute carnage on the sands of Omaha and Juno, the reality of the operation relied entirely on desperation, chance, and individual acts of remarkable grit. While senior commanders faced communication breakdowns and tactical errors miles away from the front lines, the outcome of the entire war shifted because of small groups of soldiers who refused to back down.

snippet.title: Inside the Wolf’s Lair: Hitler's Hidden Nazi Headquarters
snippet.description:
We went inside the Wolf's Lair (Wolfsschanze), Adolf Hitler’s secret Eastern Front military headquarters. Get an exclusive look at Hitler's bunker, Alfred Jodl's bunker, Hermann Goering's bunker, and Wilhelm Keitel's bunker. Explore the famous location of the Hitler assassination attempt, 'Operation Valkyrie', which almost ended the Third Reich. 

00:00:00 Introduction
00:01:53 The Wolf's Lair
00:04:12 Reich Security Service Command Centre
00:07:27 Guest Bunker
00:16:22 Alfred Jodl's Bunker
00:24:36 Hermann Goring's Bunker
00:34:39 Wilhelm Keitel's Bunker
00:43:35 20th July Plot (Operation Valkyrie)
00:54:30 Adolf Hitler's Bunker

Luke Tomes joins WW2 expert and Third Reich expert Jonny Whitlam to explore the remains of the Wolf's Lair complex today, imagining how decisions of such immense consequence were made in this remote, heavily fortified forest, and how close history came to taking a very different turn. 

During World War Two, Hitler spent most of his time in his secret bunker, making it the perfect location for a group of German officers to attempt to assassinate him. The failed Hitler assassination attempt happened on July 20 1944, in the plot known as 'Operation Valkyrie'. A bomb was detonated during a military briefing inside the complex, but Hitler survived death with only minor injuries, allowing Hitler's Nazi regime to carry on.
